questions.q: Memory has a "pick two" trade-off. If you want memory that is both low-cost and available in large quantities, what do you give up?
questions.explain: Cheap and plentiful memory is much slower, as with main memory and disk. Fast and cheap means small quantities. Fast and large means costly.

questions.q: If you want fast memory at a low cost, what is the catch?
choices: You can only get it in small quantities
It has to be accessed over a network
questions.explain: Fast and cheap is only possible in small amounts. Larger quantities would be slower or pricier.

questions.q: The memory hierarchy organizes a computer's memory devices according to which three properties?
questions.explain: The memory hierarchy is the organization of memory devices according to their speed, cost, and capacity.

questions.q: Which statements describe memory closer to the CPU (toward the top of the hierarchy)?
choices: It is more expensive per byte
It is available in smaller quantities
It holds files retrieved from remote servers
questions.explain: Closer to the CPU, memory is faster, costlier per byte, and smaller. Registers and cache are volatile, and files from remote servers are held at L5 (local disks).

questions.q: In the memory hierarchy pyramid, what does main memory (L4) hold?
choices: Cache lines retrieved from L3 cache
Disk blocks retrieved from local disks
Files retrieved from disks on remote network servers
questions.explain: Each level holds data from the level directly below it. Registers hold words, caches hold cache lines, main memory holds disk blocks, and local disks hold files from remote servers.

questions.q: Which hierarchy level (L0 through L6) is local secondary storage, such as local disks?
questions.explain: L0 registers, L1 to L3 cache (SRAM), L4 main memory (DRAM), L5 local secondary storage, L6 remote secondary storage.

questions.q: Roughly how long does an access to RAM take?
questions.explain: Registers: 0 cycles. Cache: 4 to 75 cycles. RAM: hundreds of cycles. Disk: tens of millions of cycles.

questions.q: Which storage type has an access time of about 4 to 75 cycles?
questions.explain: Cache is 4 to 75 cycles, between registers (0 cycles) and RAM (hundreds of cycles).

questions.q: Why can CPU registers be accessed with virtually zero delay?
choices: They are small flip-flops located directly on the CPU, so no bus is needed
They are built from DRAM that is refreshed constantly
They are the largest memory in the system, so data is always present
They are synchronized to both edges of the clock
questions.explain: Registers store information in simple flip-flops right on the CPU. Their small size and proximity mean no bus trip and essentially zero delay.

questions.q: Which are limitations of CPU registers?
choices: Not suited to reliable storage over long periods
Must be refreshed hundreds of times per second
Must be reached over the system bus
questions.explain: Registers are optimized for speed, not for reliable long-term storage, with minimal retention and error-checking. Refreshing is a DRAM trait, and registers need no bus.

questions.q: Each level of the memory hierarchy holds copies of data retrieved from the level directly below it.
questions.explain: In effect each level acts as a cache for the next level down.

questions.q: What does each DRAM memory cell consist of?
choices: Four to six transistors and no capacitor
A floating-gate transistor that traps electrons
questions.explain: DRAM cell = one capacitor (stores the bit) + one transistor (controls access). Four to six transistors with no capacitor describes SRAM.

questions.q: In a DRAM cell, what is the transistor's job?
choices: It stores the bit as an electrical charge
It controls access to the capacitor for reading, writing, and refreshing
It keeps the cell synchronized with the system clock
It forms a bistable circuit that holds the bit
questions.explain: The capacitor stores the bit. The transistor, a semiconductor such as silicon that can conduct or block electricity, gates access to it.

questions.q: Why is DRAM called "dynamic"?
choices: Its capacity can grow at runtime
It changes clock speed on demand
Its capacitors cannot hold charge indefinitely, so it must be refreshed hundreds of times per second
It switches between cache and main-memory roles
questions.explain: The constant refreshing needed to keep the capacitor's charge is what makes DRAM dynamic.

questions.q: To read a DRAM bit, the transistor opens access to the capacitor. If charge flows out, which bit is read?
choices: It depends on the clock edge
No value until the cell is refreshed
questions.explain: Charged capacitor = 1, so charge flowing out reads as 1. No charge reads as 0.

questions.q: SRAM's transistors form a circuit that can stably hold either of two states as long as power is supplied. What is this kind of circuit called?
questions.explain: A bistable circuit: high-voltage state = 1, low-voltage state = 0.

questions.q: Because SRAM does not need to be refreshed, it keeps its data even when power is removed.
questions.explain: SRAM is still volatile. It holds its state only as long as power is supplied. "Static" only means no refresh is needed.

questions.q: Why is SRAM faster and more stable than DRAM?
choices: No time is spent charging, discharging, and refreshing capacitors
There is no charge leakage, so there is less risk of data loss or corruption
It is stored on remote servers with redundancy
It uses only one transistor per cell
questions.explain: SRAM has no capacitor, so it skips the capacitor's charge/discharge/refresh time and has no leakage.

questions.q: Which pairing of RAM type and typical use is correct?
choices: SRAM for main memory, DRAM for cache
SRAM for cache, DRAM for main memory
SRAM for local disks, DRAM for registers
Both are used only for secondary storage
questions.explain: SRAM is used for L1 to L3 cache. DRAM is used for main memory (L4).

questions.q: In SRAM, how is a 1 bit represented?
choices: A high-voltage state of the bistable circuit
A floating gate full of electrons
questions.explain: In SRAM, high voltage = 1 and low voltage = 0. A charged capacitor is DRAM's representation.

questions.q: "Random access" means any item can be accessed in constant time without traversing other items first.
questions.explain: That is the meaning of random access in RAM.

questions.q: Physically, what is the capacitor in a DRAM cell?
choices: Two conductive plates separated by a non-conductive, insulating material
A loop of four to six transistors
A silicon gate that traps electrons
questions.explain: One plate holds positive charge and one holds negative charge, with insulation between them. It briefly stores and releases charge.

questions.q: What distinguishes SDRAM from earlier DRAM?
choices: It operates in sync with the system clock
It uses capacitors instead of transistors
questions.explain: Synchronous DRAM is DRAM that operates in sync with the system clock.

questions.q: What problem did asynchronous DRAM cause?
choices: It lost data on every clock tick
It carried out commands on its own internal timing, so the CPU might have to wait, creating a bottleneck between the CPU and main memory
It could be read but never written
It required a network connection to operate
questions.explain: The memory controller sent commands, but the DRAM executed them on its own schedule. The CPU could stall waiting, reducing performance.

questions.q: Why wasn't DRAM synchronized with the system clock from the start?
choices: Early CPUs were slower and computers were costlier, so syncing was not considered necessary or feasible
The system clock had not yet been invented
Synchronizing would have made DRAM non-volatile
SRAM already handled all main-memory traffic
questions.explain: The bottleneck only became noticeable, and therefore a problem, as computers became more efficient.

questions.q: How does DDR SDRAM double the work done per clock cycle?
choices: It performs one operation on the rising edge and one on the falling edge of each clock tick
It doubles the number of capacitors per cell
questions.explain: Each clock tick has a rising and a falling edge. DDR does one operation on each, making it twice as fast as earlier SDRAM.

questions.q: How many operations does DDR SDRAM perform per clock cycle?
questions.explain: One on the rising edge and one on the falling edge.

questions.q: DRAM that ran on its own timing, before SDRAM, is sometimes called by what abbreviation?
questions.explain: ADRAM, asynchronous DRAM.

questions.q: What does the system clock do?
choices: Stores the date and time in non-volatile memory
Generates pulses that coordinate operations across the computer
Decides which cache line to evict
questions.explain: For example, each tick might correspond to one step of the fetch-and-execute cycle.

questions.q: Before SDRAM, which component sent read/write commands to the DRAM?
questions.explain: The memory controller sent commands, and the DRAM carried them out on its own internal timing.

questions.q: DDR2, DDR3, DDR4, and DDR5 are successive improvements on DDR SDRAM.
questions.explain: They all build on double data rate SDRAM, which most computers use today.

questions.q: Around what year did SDRAM arrive, ending the era of DRAM running on its own timing?
questions.explain: About 1992.

questions.q: Both local and remote secondary storage are non-volatile.
questions.explain: Their data remains after the program ends and/or power is removed. That is why they are also called permanent storage.

questions.q: Compared with remote secondary storage, local secondary storage has:
choices: The same latency, since both use disks
questions.explain: Local storage is connected directly to the machine. Remote storage depends on a network, which makes it slower and less reliable.

questions.q: Remote secondary storage is slower and less reliable than local storage. Which benefits does it often offer in exchange?
questions.explain: Remote storage (such as Google Drive, AWS, Dropbox) trades speed and reliability for cost-effectiveness, scalability, and remote access.

questions.q: Which are examples of local secondary storage?
questions.explain: Local storage connects directly: HDDs, SSDs, external drives, optical discs. Google Drive and Dropbox are cloud (remote) storage.

questions.q: In a hard disk drive, what is seek time?
choices: Time for the arm to move the head to the correct location (track)
Time for the disk to spin the correct location under the head
Time to actually read or write the data
Time for the OS to find the file in its directory
questions.explain: Seek time = the arm moves. Rotational latency = waiting for the spin. Transfer time = the actual read or write.

questions.q: In a hard disk drive, what is rotational latency?
choices: Time for the arm to move the head to the correct location (track)
Time for the disk to spin the correct location under the head
Time to actually read or write the data
Time for the OS to find the file in its directory
questions.explain: The platter spins at a fixed rate, so after the seek you wait for the right spot to rotate under the head.

questions.q: Which HDD access delays does an SSD avoid entirely?
questions.explain: SSDs have no moving parts, so there is no arm to move and no platter to spin. Data still has to be transferred.

questions.q: How does an HDD read a bit?
choices: The read/write head detects the magnetic polarization of a grain on the platter
The head measures charge flowing out of a capacitor
A floating gate releases trapped electrons
A bistable circuit is sampled for high or low voltage
questions.explain: HDDs store bits by magnetizing grains on a spinning disk. Reading detects the polarization, and writing changes it.

questions.q: How do SSDs store information?
choices: NAND flash memory: floating-gate transistors that trap electrons
Capacitors refreshed hundreds of times per second
questions.explain: SSDs store information as trapped electrical signals using NAND flash memory.

questions.q: In the NAND flash model presented in this module, what does a floating gate containing trapped electrons represent?
questions.explain: In this material, a gate containing electrons = 1 and an empty gate = 0. (Real flash devices often label these the other way around, but this is the convention the material uses.)

questions.q: Which are disadvantages of SSDs compared with HDDs?
choices: They wear out more quickly because of how they write data
Recovering data from them is much more difficult
They are more prone to mechanical failure
questions.explain: SSDs use less power and fail mechanically less often because nothing spins. Their downsides are faster wear and harder data recovery.

questions.q: NAND flash memory resembles a NAND logic gate in structure and also functions exactly like one.
questions.explain: The structure resembles a NOT AND gate, but it does not function like one.

questions.q: What is it called when an HDD's arm moves radially to position the read/write head over a particular track?
questions.explain: A seek. The time it takes is the seek time.

questions.q: An HDD's read/write head flies over the disk surface on a thin cushion of air.
questions.explain: The head sits at the end of the arm and flies just above the spinning platter.

questions.q: What is temporal locality?
choices: If a program accesses an address, it is likely to access that same address again soon
If a program accesses an address, it is likely to access nearby addresses soon
Programs tend to access memory in random order
Data that has been in memory longer is accessed more often
questions.explain: Temporal = same place, again soon. Spatial = nearby place, soon.

questions.q: What is spatial locality?
choices: If a program accesses an address, it is likely to access that same address again soon
If a program accesses an address, it is likely to access nearby addresses soon
Programs tend to access memory in random order
Data that has been in memory longer is accessed more often
questions.explain: Spatial locality is about nearby addresses, such as walking through an array.

questions.q: In the loop  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) total += a[i];  the variable total is read and written on every iteration. Which kind of locality does that illustrate?
questions.explain: The same address (total) is reused again and again, which is temporal locality.

questions.q: Walking through an array one element after another, in storage order, is a classic example of which kind of locality?
questions.explain: Each access is to an address next to the previous one, which is spatial locality.

questions.q: How does the operating system exploit locality?
choices: By using RAM as a cache for disk, keeping recently referenced items in RAM
By choosing big endian byte order
By converting column-major arrays to row-major
questions.explain: The OS keeps the most recently referenced items in RAM to avoid slow disk access. This involves paging and virtual address space.

questions.q: At which layers is the principle of locality exploited?
choices: Hardware (keeping recently referenced blocks in cache)
Operating system (using RAM as a cache for disk)
questions.explain: Locality is exploited in hardware, the operating system, and applications.

questions.q: Program A fills array[1000] and then immediately sums it. Program B fills array[1000], then fills a second new_array[1000], then sums array. Why is B likely slower when it sums array?
choices: The work in between risks evicting array from cache, so the sum causes more misses
Summing requires new_array to be refreshed first
B stores array in column-major order
B has a larger stride when summing
questions.explain: B has bad temporal locality: by the time array is reused, it may no longer be in cache. A reuses the data right away while it is still cached.

questions.q: A program that reuses data soon after loading it has good temporal locality, because the data is likely still in cache.
questions.explain: Using data again as soon as possible after loading it keeps accesses in fast cache.

questions.q: Why is it useful to be able to predict which memory a program will access next?
choices: So the data can be loaded into faster storage ahead of time, avoiding long RAM and disk access times
So the OS can delete files that will not be used
So DRAM refreshes can be skipped
So the CPU can switch endianness
questions.explain: Locality makes that prediction possible, which lets the hierarchy keep the right data in fast memory.

questions.q: How do C and C++ lay out a 2D array such as int m[R][C] in memory?
choices: As separate rows scattered around memory
In whatever order the program first accesses it
questions.explain: C-family languages store the whole of row 0, then row 1, and so on, as one contiguous series.

questions.q: Which sequence is the column-major storage order of a 3x3 matrix?
questions.explain: Column-major stores column 0 completely, then column 1, then column 2. The first option is row-major.

questions.q: In C++, which loop over int m[R][C] has good spatial locality?
choices: Outer loop over i (rows), inner loop over j (columns), accessing m[i][j]
Outer loop over j (columns), inner loop over i (rows), accessing m[i][j]
Both are equally good, because RAM access is constant time
Neither, because 2D arrays are not stored contiguously
questions.explain: Row-wise iteration visits elements in the order they are stored (stride-1). In C/C++, the innermost loop should vary the last index.

questions.q: Column-wise iteration over a 3x3 matrix stored in row-major order has a stride-k reference pattern. What is k?
questions.explain: Each step down a column skips a full row of 3 elements, so it is stride-3.

questions.q: What stride does column-wise iteration have over a row-major matrix declared int m[6][8] (6 rows, 8 columns)?
questions.explain: Column-wise iteration over a row-major R x C matrix is stride-C. Here C = 8.

questions.q: What stride does row-wise iteration over a row-major matrix have?
questions.explain: Row-wise iteration visits each element in storage order, which is stride-1, the best case for spatial locality.

questions.q: In a 3x3 matrix stored in row-major order, at what 0-based position in the flat sequence is a12 stored?
For the row-major array int m[6][8], at what 0-based position in the flat sequence is m[2][3] stored?
questions.explain: Position = i * C + j = 2 * 8 + 3 = 19.

questions.q: In a 3x3 matrix stored in column-major order, at what 0-based position is a12 (row 1, column 2) stored?
questions.explain: Column-major: a00, a10, a20, a01, a11, a21, a02, a12, a22. a12 is at position 7.

questions.q: In a 3x3 matrix stored in row-major order, which element comes immediately after a02 in memory?
questions.explain: Row 0 ends at a02, and row 1 begins with a10.

questions.q: Column-wise iteration over a row-major matrix has bad spatial locality because it keeps jumping along the array.
questions.explain: It visits a00, a10, a20, a01, ..., skipping a row's worth of elements on each step.

questions.q: To access the "center" element of a 3x3 matrix, which row and column do you use?
questions.explain: Indices start at 0, so the middle of 0, 1, 2 is 1.

questions.q: Why is cache memory needed between the registers and main memory?
choices: Registers are too small to hold much information, and main memory is too slow for optimal performance
Main memory is non-volatile and cannot be written quickly
Registers must be accessed over the bus
questions.explain: Cache fills the gap. Because the CPU often reuses the same or nearby data, keeping it in cache saves time.

questions.q: Moving toward the CPU (L3 to L2 to L1), each cache level is larger and slower than the one before it.
questions.explain: Moving toward the CPU, each level is smaller and faster and holds data the CPU accesses more frequently.

questions.q: Where is cache memory most often located?
choices: Directly on the CPU chip, or on a separate chip very close by
questions.explain: Cache is high-speed memory located near the CPU.

questions.q: What is the typical size range of a cache line?
questions.explain: Cache lines are fixed and small, typically 16 to 256 bytes.

questions.q: The CPU requests data from one memory address that is not in cache. What gets loaded into cache?
choices: The entire cache line containing that address
The whole matrix row being accessed
questions.explain: The whole cache line comes in, so the requested byte's neighbors are already cached.

questions.q: Fetching whole cache lines at once helps a program take advantage of which kind of locality?
questions.explain: Nearby data arrives along with the requested data, so later accesses to neighbors hit. That is spatial locality.

questions.q: What happens on a cache miss?
choices: The data is fetched from main memory, a new cache line is loaded into cache, and the data is sent to the CPU
The data is sent directly to the CPU from cache
questions.explain: A miss is the suboptimal case. On a hit, the data goes straight from cache to the CPU.

questions.q: What is the miss penalty?
choices: The fraction of memory references that miss
The additional time required when a miss occurs
The number of lines evicted per miss
The extra hardware cost of adding cache
questions.explain: Miss penalty = how much performance is lost per miss. The fraction that miss is the miss rate.

questions.q: A program makes 200 memory references and 30 of them miss. What is the hit rate, as a decimal?
A program's hit rate is 0.93. What is its miss rate, as a decimal?
questions.explain: Every reference either hits or misses, so hit rate + miss rate = 1.

questions.q: Suppose a cache line is 64 bytes and an int is 4 bytes. How many ints fit in one cache line?
With 64-byte cache lines and 4-byte ints, a stride-1 scan of a large int array misses only on the first access to each line. What is the miss rate, as a decimal?
questions.explain: Each line holds 16 ints: 1 miss followed by 15 hits, so the miss rate is 1/16 = 0.0625.

questions.q: Registers, cache, and main memory all offer constant-time access. Why does the order in which a program touches data still affect performance?
choices: What matters is where in the hierarchy the data currently lives. In-order access turns more accesses into cache hits and avoids slow trips to RAM over the bus.
Constant-time access only applies to the first access of each item
Out-of-order access forces DRAM to switch endianness
In-order access lets the CPU skip refresh cycles
questions.explain: Each device is constant time, but cache (4 to 75 cycles) and RAM (hundreds of cycles) differ hugely. Fewer reads from slower memory means less time spent and less bus traffic.

questions.q: Components other than the CPU, such as disk drives, can have their own cache memory.
questions.explain: For example, an SSD contains its own cache chip.

questions.q: Which cache line does LRU (Least Recently Used) evict?
choices: The line that was accessed least recently
The line that was loaded earliest
The line that was accessed most often
questions.explain: LRU evicts by last use, not by load time.

questions.q: Which cache line does FIFO (First-In, First-Out) evict?
choices: The line that was accessed least recently
The line that was loaded earliest
The line that was accessed most often
questions.explain: FIFO evicts by age: the oldest-loaded line goes first, however recently it was used.

questions.q: Which replacement policy is the quickest because it does zero tracking, making it a good fit for L1 cache?
questions.explain: Random replacement has no bookkeeping, so it is fast. However, it is unpredictable and cannot be optimized.

questions.q: Which replacement policy rewards strong temporal locality but is more complex to implement?
questions.explain: LRU keeps recently used lines, which rewards reuse, but it must track usage.

questions.q: Which replacement policy is simple to implement but can punish temporal locality?
questions.explain: FIFO may evict a line that was loaded long ago but is still heavily used.

questions.q: A cache holds 2 lines and starts empty. The access sequence is X, Y, X, Z, X. How many hits occur under LRU?
questions.explain: X miss, Y miss, X hit, Z miss (evicts Y, the least recently used), X hit. 2 hits.

questions.q: A cache holds 2 lines and starts empty. The access sequence is X, Y, X, Z, X. How many hits occur under FIFO?
questions.explain: X miss, Y miss, X hit, Z miss (evicts X, the oldest loaded), X miss. 1 hit.

questions.q: A cache holds 3 lines and starts empty. The access sequence is A, B, A, C, A, D, A. How many hits occur under LRU?
questions.explain: A miss, B miss, A hit, C miss, A hit, D miss (evicts B, the least recently used), A hit. 3 hits.

questions.q: A 3-line cache starts empty and sees A, B, A, C, A, D. Under FIFO, which line is evicted to make room for D?
questions.explain: A was loaded first, so FIFO evicts it even though it is used constantly. LRU would have evicted B instead.

questions.q: Random replacement is predictable and can be tuned to a program's access pattern.
questions.explain: Random replacement is unpredictable and cannot be optimized. Its advantage is speed.

questions.q: Why does a cache need a replacement policy at all?
choices: When a miss brings a new line into the cache, an older line must be overwritten
To decide when DRAM cells are refreshed
To choose between big and little endian
To decide which disk track to seek to
questions.explain: Cache is small. The replacement policy decides which existing line gets evicted.

questions.q: What does "endianness" refer to?
choices: The order in which a system stores and/or interprets bytes
The order of bits within a cache tag
The direction a disk platter spins
The order in which cache lines are evicted
questions.explain: Endianness is byte order for values that span multiple addresses.

questions.q: In a big endian system, which byte of a multi-byte value is stored at the lowest address?
choices: Whichever byte is accessed most often
questions.explain: Big endian puts the big end (MSB) first. Little endian puts the LSB first.

questions.q: The 4-byte value 0x12345678 is stored starting at address 0x200 on a little endian machine. Which byte is at address 0x200?
questions.explain: Little endian puts the least significant byte first: 78 56 34 12 at 0x200 to 0x203.

questions.q: Which byte sequence shows 0xA1B2C3D4 stored big endian at addresses 0x10 through 0x13 (lowest address first)?
questions.explain: Big endian stores MSB to LSB, the same order you write the number. Little endian would be D4 C3 B2 A1.

questions.q: A little endian machine shows the bytes EF BE AD DE at increasing addresses. What 32-bit value is stored, in hex?
questions.explain: Reverse the byte order (not the digits): DE AD BE EF, which is 0xDEADBEEF.

questions.q: How is the 2-byte value 0x1234 stored in little endian (lowest address first)?
questions.explain: Endianness reverses bytes, not hex digits. Each byte keeps its normal internal order.

questions.q: Which byte order makes increments, addition/subtraction, and even/odd checks simpler and faster?
choices: Neither; they are identical for arithmetic
questions.explain: Little endian always has the least significant byte first, which is where arithmetic and parity checks start.

questions.q: Which byte order is easier for humans to read and makes comparing value sizes and checking the sign bit easier in hardware?
questions.explain: Big endian matches how people write numbers, and the most significant byte (containing the sign bit) sits at the lowest address.

questions.q: On a big endian machine, an 8-byte long holding decimal 5 is mistakenly read as a 4-byte int from the same starting address. What value is read?
questions.explain: Big endian layout: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 05. The first four bytes are all 00, so the int reads 0 instead of 5.

questions.q: An 8-byte long holding 5 is mistakenly read as a 4-byte int from the same starting address. Under which byte order is the value still read correctly as 5?
questions.explain: Little endian layout: 05 00 00 00 00 00 00 00. The first four bytes, 05 00 00 00, read least to most significant, give 00000005 = 5.

questions.q: The 8-byte value 01 23 FE ED BA BE F0 0D is stored little endian at addresses 0x01 through 0x08. Which byte is at address 0x04?
questions.explain: Little endian layout: 0D F0 BE BA ED FE 23 01 at 0x01 to 0x08, so 0x04 holds BA.

questions.q: Where do the terms "big endian" and "little endian" come from?
choices: Gulliver's Travels by Jonathan Swift, where the Lilliputians fight over which end of a hard-boiled egg to eat first
The surnames of two early CPU designers
Whether the outer or inner edge of a disk platter is read first
An early networking standard's names for packet headers
questions.explain: Swift (1726): big-endians eat the big end of the egg first, and little-endians eat the little end first.

questions.q: The choice between big and little endian is unimportant in most cases, as long as every part of the system or network uses the same endianness.
questions.explain: Endianness only causes trouble when machines that disagree exchange data without translation.

questions.q: Two machines use different endianness. What can translate the byte order so they don't misread each other's data?
questions.explain: Byte-order translation can be handled by the OS, software, special libraries, and so on.

questions.q: Little endian reverses the order of the hex digits inside each byte as well as the order of the bytes.
questions.explain: Only the byte order is reversed. Little endian is read right-to-left across bytes but left-to-right within a byte.

questions.q: In modern computers, each memory address refers to 1 byte (8 bits) of data.
questions.explain: That is why any value larger than one byte must be spread across several consecutive addresses, which raises the question of byte order.
